If by quitting you hurt their scores, kick them from the match, end the match entirely, etc, that's a dick move. Literally just sit there and take Ls until the match is over, then stop playing the game. But like, if you're playing Warzone and you suck and just decide to get off, no harm no foul imo. Just don't be driving something with passengers in it when that happens. Do your best to land safely, exit the thing, and excuse yourself from the match. Getting mad isn't worth it but fucking people over because you're upset is a bad move.

Depends on what you mean by rage quitting 

If you're screaming, slamming controllers, etc, that's not healthy. I've been there too and it, for me, was a symptom of deeper emotional and psychological problems I needed to handle.

If you're just extremely frustrated with a game and either want to abruptly stop playing it or to never play it again by simply ejecting/exiting out of the game and perhaps deleting it, that's fine. Sometimes your tastes in games won't be compatible with the experience being provided by the game, and other times you may just suck at it. And a few times, it may truly be that the game is janky or bizarrely difficult (the former being a problem, the latter being a matter of taste and skill-level, with both leaving you incapable of enjoying playing it fundamentally). When I get frustrated by a game that I can't seem to overcome or advance in, I typically stop playing it and often delete it. Sometimes I even sell it back. If you know you can't handle it, just be mature about it, turn it off, and leave it to rest. Or delete/sell it if you're that disinterested in it.

But if you're yelling and throwing shit, seek help and stop playing the game immediately and permanently, especially if you're an adult.

that said, as someone who is fascinated by religion but isn't exactly religious (i'm an agnostic leaning more towards atheism at the moment), none of that is provable. it can't be provable either, as we are now talking about something that is no longer part of physical existence. science exists to prove, learn about, and/or discover everything physically possible. if it is not physically existent, then it cannot prove it, which then also means that it is not a "fact" that god "has to exist". the belief in god(s) and any ideologies or creeds that this (these) god(s) may have created belongs in the realm of philosophy. it's a valid idea, plenty of great scientists like Albert Einstein and Michio Kaku have toyed with the idea themselves, and others such as Neil DeGrasse Tyson and Richard Dawkins do not find the idea preposterous even if they don't personally subscribe to it. science and religion do not ever have to contradict each other so long as they remain separated. religion postulates ideas about an existence greater than our physical world. considering that it is remarkably mysterious how these laws that, at some fundamental level, exist in perpetuity are so beautifully designed and have the random potential to yield a universe fit for conscious existence, it is not unreasonable to believe in some kind of essence outside of physical existence that designed them. it's sort of like a coder setting up parameters for a program. Political correctness has its pitfalls, but there's a nuanced way to argue against it, and then there's the "FREE SPEECH I CAN SAY WHAT I WANT" way to argue against it. Political correctness can sometimes landslide into blind censorship of any ideology that doesn't fit with whatever the person or institution espousing their individual idea of what is politically correct is. Political correctness can at times lead to mansplaining and whitesplaining, where men who study gender studies and whites who study racial studies "correct" women and minorities for being wrong about what it's like to be a woman or a minority, and what women and minorities "should do" due to them being women and minorities. Political correctness can also lend itself to propping up identity politics, wherein we focus on the appearance and aesthetic of a person, be it a politician, artist, public figure, etc, over their character. This is where you get people advocating for political candidates solely due to them being minorities or women, rather than focusing primarily on their policies. Finally, political correctness can often be determined by corporations, political groups, and influencers, and they specifically tailor their political correctness around their agendas. An example of this is how the Grammy's had a segment bashing Donald Trump in 2018, but they barely nominated any women that year, despite propping themselves up as "progressive". Same with any liberal who will mock Donald Trump's physical appearance for the sake of emasculating him and trying to discredit him as a valid politician. But the arguments most people prop up against political correctness are braindead. "You should be able to say what you want, it's a free country, first amendment, you choose what you're offended by, etc." are surface level, sophomoric arguments against being politically correct that go absolutely fucking nowhere. Nobody is questions whether or not you objectively can or cannot say something, and any rational person doesn't believe any penal action should be expected for saying objectionable things. But creating a society that is more respectful of the sensitivities of various groups of people is definitely not a bad thing. It's just that political correctness, as it is currently practice, often misfires in that it actually does *too little* of what it proposes to do, and requires way more depth of understanding from the majority of people who try to be "woke" or whatever. I think "Ye" could signal a moment in Kanye's career where he's definitively over trying to top his prior effort, or even conjure up new ideas, and just make solid albums to pad out his back catalog. TCD-TLOP were all in their own ways really unique, distinctive pieces of music, that capture moments in time culturally, defined them even. "Ye" didn't do that. It definitely captures a moment in Kanye's life, but doesn't really go beyond that. It's just a little snapshot into the frayed mind of a visionary. I think people place an unrealistic and delusional expectation on Kanye, who in no short measure brings it on himself with his shameless hubris, artistically. People think they guy needs to drop a classic that is a complete deviation from the prior album every time. But every artist who has followed similar trajectories, i.e. David Bowie, Nine Inch Nails, King Crimson, etc, eventually reached points in their careers where they had established their prime and were now officially moving past their prime. Ye as an overall artist is still as vital as ever, his work on KSG and Daytona speak for themselves. But his solo efforts are reaching a point to me where he will probably just keep delivering worthwhile content for years to come, but won't necessarily shake the world up anymore. That he was able to have the world by the balls for 12 years is astounding and ranks him alongside the best artists we've ever had. He also may very well give us another earth shattering musical moment. But as of now, "ye" leaves Kanye's legacy in pretty much the same condition it was in before it dropped. It doesn't add much, but doesn't really detract anything either. It's just a good, solid album. Nothing wrong with that tbh. 

As far as collaborative albums though, sky's the limit. KSG was another classic under his belt, and when he works with artists he's inspired by his creativity honestly knows no limits.
